extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, physicists, and historians of science (readers of Newtonian classical mechanics; Latin-literate scholars)
extracted.subtask_description: Extraction of propositions and theorems from a Latin section of a classical mechanics treatise (motion under centripetal/mutual attraction), with their statements and surrounding explanatory corollaries and constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. LIII. Prob. XXXV — Isochronous oscillations in given curved lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Concessis figurarum curvilinearum Quadraturis, invenire vires quibus corpora in datis curvis lineis Oscillationes semper Isochronas peragent. (Given the quadratures of curved figures, find the forces by which bodies moving in given curved lines will always execute isochronous oscillations.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: at a point T on curve STRQ take tangent TX and an arc-equal TY to TR; from Y draw YZ perpendicular to the tangent, and CT meeting at Z; the centripetal force is proportional to TZ. Demonstration resolves the actual force into TY and YZ components: YZ acting along the string length doesn't change motion, TY accelerates/retards motion along the curve. Hence if TY relates to the sine of half-arc TR in a given way, the oscillation times are equal. Corollaries discuss the circular pendulum special case (relation of TR to its sine TN) and application to clocks: if machine-exerted forces on a pendulum combine with gravity so that total downward force is as the rectangle under arc TR and radius AR to sine TN, oscillations are isochronous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. LIV. Prob. XXXVI — Times of descent/ascent on planar curves under given centripetal force
rubrics_metrics.description: Concessis figurarum curvilinearum quadraturis, invenire tempora quibus corpora vi qualibet centripeta in lineis quibuscunq; curvis in plano per centrum virium transeunte descriptis, descendent & ascendent. (Given quadratures and the law of centripetal force toward a given center, to find the times in which bodies descend and ascend along arbitrary plane curves passing through the force-center.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method: divide CS into many equal parts; at each subinterval CD describe circles with center C cutting the curve at points; using Proposition XXXIX give the velocity at any radius CT. The time to traverse a small element Tt is proportional to its length divided by velocity; mapping that time to a perpendicular DN at D gives a rectangle Dd×DN (area DNnd) proportional to the local time. The envelope curve SNn whose areas correspond to these DN areas yields total area SNDS proportional to the time of descent along ST. Thus from the constructed area one obtains the time. (Q.E.I.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. LV. Theor. XIX — Projection-area proportionality for motion on curved surface
rubrics_metrics.description: Si corpus movetur in superficie quacunq; curva, cujus axis per centrum virium transit, eiq; parallela & æqualis ab axis puncto quovis ducatur: dico quod parallela illa aream tempori proportionalem describet. (If a body moves on any curved surface whose axis passes through the center of forces, and from the body a perpendicular to the axis is drawn and a line equal and parallel to it from any point on the axis, that parallel will describe an area proportional to time.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Setup: project the trajectory onto a plane AOP by taking the foot P of perpendicular from trajectory point to the axis and follow its locus AP. Resolve forces into components tangent and normal to the surface; the normal components only affect motion perpendicular to the plane and may be neglected for planar motion of the projection. Thus the projection AP in plane AOP is described by centripetal forces toward O, and by Prop. I the area AOP described by the radius OP is proportional to time. Corollary: same argument extends to multiple centers on same line (areas remain proportional to time).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. LVI. Prob. XXXVII — Trajectory on given curved surface from initial data
rubrics_metrics.description: Concessis figurarum curvilinearum Quadraturis, datisq; tum lege vis centripetæ ad centrum datum tendentis, tum superficie curva cujus axis per centrum illud transit; invenienda est Trajectoria quam corpus in eadem superficie describet, de loco dato, data cum velocitate versus plagam in superficie illa datam egressum. (Given quadratures, the law of centripetal force to a given center, and a curved surface whose axis passes through that center; find the trajectory described by a body on that surface from a given point with a given initial velocity in a given direction.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method: from the given speed at altitude SC compute velocity at other altitudes TC; with minimal time the body describes a small arc Tt whose projection Pp in plane AOP is an elliptic arc PpQ determined by a circle described in the surface with center T and radius Tt. Because area PO p is proportional to time, the position Op is known, yielding intersection p of ellipse and circle; repeating produces APp the projected locus, then erecting perpendiculars PT to the surface yields actual trajectory points T. (Construction reduces to problems used in Prop. XLI.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Sect. XI — Principle: mutual attractions and common center motion
rubrics_metrics.description: Hactenus exposui motus corporum attractorum ad centrum immobile... Attractiones enim fieri solent ad corpora; & corporum trahentium & attractorum actiones semper mutuæ sunt & æquales, per Legem tertiam: adeo ut neq; attrahens possit quiescere neq; attractum... (General explanation that real bodies attract each other, their actions are mutual and equal, and thus two attracting bodies revolve about their common center of gravity; if more bodies, the common center either rests or moves uniformly.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author adopts treating centripetal forces as mutual attractions (impulses) for mathematical exposition, with corollaries: the common center may be at rest or move uniformly; motions can be analyzed by replacing mutual attractions by attraction to a single body at the common center with appropriate law, simplifying many-body problems to single-center problems under hypotheses stated later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. LVII. Theor. XX — Two mutually attracting bodies describe similar figures
rubrics_metrics.description: Corpora duo se invicem trahentia describunt, & circum commune centrum gravitatis, & circum se mutuo, figuras similes. (Two bodies attracting each other describe similar figures about their common center of gravity and about each other.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: distances from the common center are reciprocally proportional to the bodies and thus preserve given ratios; straight lines in given ratios swept by equal angular motion produce similar figures in the respective frames. Hence the figures traced about the common center and about each other are similar. (Q.E.D.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. LVIII. Theor. XXI — Motion about each other equivalent to motion about fixed center
rubrics_metrics.description: Si corpora duo viribus quibusvis se mutuo trahunt, & interea revolvuntur circa gravitatis centrum commune: dico quod figuris, quas corpora sic mota describunt circum se mutuo, potest figura similis & æqualis, circum corpus alterutrum immotum, viribus iisdem describi. (If two bodies attract each other and revolve about their common center, then the figure one describes about the other while both move can be equal and similar to the figure it would describe about the other if that other were fixed and the same forces acted.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by constructing equal parallel displacements sp, sq and showing similarity of resulting curves; two cases considered: (1) center at rest, (2) center moving uniformly — in both cases similarity holds. Corollaries: (1) two bodies with forces proportional to their masses describe concentric ellipses; (2) inverse-square forces give conic sections with common focus; (3) areas described by radii to the common center are proportional to times.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. LIX. Theor. XXII — Relation of periods for mutual motion vs. one-body motion
rubrics_metrics.description: Corporum duorum S & P circa commune gravitatis centrum C revolventium tempus periodicum esse ad tempus periodicum corporis alterutrius P, circa alterum immotum S gyrantis & figuris quæ corpora circum se mutuo describunt figuram similem & æqualem describentis, in dimidiata ratione corporis alterius S, ad summam corporum S + P. (The periodic time of two bodies S and P about their common center relates to the periodic time of P about a fixed S — when the two describe similar and equal figures — in the subduplicate/half ratio of the other body S to the sum S+P.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From previous theorem: times for similar arcs are in a half ratio of distances to center, which translates to the stated mass-sum ratio. Thus total periods of similar figures are in the same subduplicate ratio. (Q.E.D.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. LX. Theor. XXIII — Relation of transverse axes for ellipses under mutual inverse-square attraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Si corpora duo S & P, viribus quadrato distantiæ suæ reciproce proportionalibus se mutuo trahentia, revolvuntur circa gravitatis centrum commune: dico quod Ellipseos, quam corpus alterutrum P hoc motu circa alterum S describit, Axis transversus erit ad axem transversum Ellipseos, quam corpus idem P circa alterum quiescens S eodem tempore periodico describere posset, ut summa corporum duorum S + P ad primam duarum medie proportionalium inter hanc summam & corpus illud alterum S ad S + P. (For two bodies under inverse-square attraction, the transverse axis of the ellipse described in the mutual case compares to that described if one were fixed in the ratio indicated involving the sum of the masses and the mean proportionals.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof outlines reduction via equality/inequality of axes and periods; changing mass ratios alters period and transverse axis according to the derived proportion (involving two mean proportionals). Inverse statements also given: axis ratios invert accordingly. (Q.E.D.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. LXI. Theor. XXIV — Equivalence of mutual attraction to attraction to a single body at common center
rubrics_metrics.description: Si corpora duo viribus quibusvis se mutuo trahentia, neq; alias agitata vel impedita, quomodocunq; moveantur; motus eorum perinde se habebunt ac si non traherent se mutuo, sed utrumq; a corpore tertio in communi gravitatis centro constituto viribus iisdem traheretur: Et Virium trahentium eadem erit Lex respectu distantiæ corporum a centro illo communi atq; respectu distantiæ totius inter corpora. (If two mutually attracting bodies move however they please without other forces, their motion will be the same as if they were attracted by a third body at the common center with the same law: the attracting forces obey the same distance law relative to that center and relative to the total distance between the bodies.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reason: mutual forces tending to each other can be considered as tending to the intermediate common center; thus motions may be treated as single-center problems with an equivalent law. This gives a powerful reduction for analysis. (Q.E.D.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. LXII. Prob. XXXVIII — Determine motions for inverse-square mutual attraction with given initial places
rubrics_metrics.description: Corporum duorum quæ viribus quadrato distantiæ suæ reciproce proportionalibus se mutuo trahunt, ac de locis datis demittuntur, determinare motus. (Determine motions of two bodies attracting each other by inverse-square forces, given their initial positions.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By Theorem LXI reduce problem to motion under forces toward a fixed center at the common center (which by hypothesis remains at rest). Use Problem XXV to determine motions as if attracted by forces to that center. (Q.E.I.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. LXIII. Prob. XXXIX — Determine motions for inverse-square mutual attraction with given lines and velocities
rubrics_metrics.description: Corporum duorum quæ viribus quadrato distantiæ suæ reciproce proportionalibus se mutuo trahunt, deq; locis datis, secundum datas rectas, datis cum velocitatibus exeunt, determinare motus. (Determine the motions of two bodies under inverse-square mutual attraction given their initial positions, given initial straight directions and velocities.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separate uniform motion of common center from motions relative to it (per Legum Corollaria and Theorem LXI). Reduce to the single-center problems solved by earlier Problems (Nos. 9 and 26). Compose the relative motions with uniform system motion to obtain absolute motions in fixed space. (Q.E.D.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. LXIV. Prob. XL — Motions when attraction toward centers increases in simple ratio of distances
rubrics_metrics.description: Viribus quibus Corpora se mutuo trahunt crescentibus in simplici ratione distantiarum a centris: requiruntur motus plurium Corporum inter se. (When the mutual attracting forces increase in the simple ratio of distances from their centers, find the motions of several bodies among themselves.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start with two bodies T & L with common center D describing ellipses; add a third body S attracting them with accelerative forces ST, SL; resolve these forces and show that T & L still describe ellipses about D (but with faster motion); S describes an ellipse about its own center C, etc. Adding more bodies proceeds similarly: system can be composed of elliptic motions about successive centers. (Q.E.I.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. LXV. Theor. XXV — Approximate elliptic motion and area-time proportionality for many bodies under inverse-square law
rubrics_metrics.description: Corpora plura quorum vires decrescunt in duplicata ratione distantiarum ab eorundem centris, moveri posse inter se in Ellipsibus, & radiis ad umbilicos ductis Areas describere temporibus proportionales quam proxime. (Many bodies whose forces decrease in the duplicate ratio of distances may move among themselves in ellipses and sweep areas about focal points approximately proportional to times.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The precise elliptic motion holds in idealized cases; in realistic multi-body systems perturbations cause deviations. Two cases discussed: (1) many small bodies around a dominant mass approximate ellipses about that mass if the small bodies' influences are negligible; (2) a system of small bodies plus two large ones moving uniformly yields nearly exact elliptic motion if inclination and unequal accelerative forces are small. Errors can be made arbitrarily small by decreasing the small masses. Corollaries discuss dependence of perturbation on mass ratios and geometry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. LXVI. Theor. XXVI — Three-body perturbations and conditions for near-elliptic areas proportional to times
rubrics_metrics.description: Si corpora tria, quorum vires decrescunt in duplicata ratione distantiarum, se mutuo trahant, & attractiones acceleratrices binorum quorumcunq; in tertium sint inter se reciproce ut quadrata distantiarum; minora autem circa maximum in plano communi revolvantur: Dico quod interius circa intimum & maximum, radiis ad ipsum ductis, describet areas temporibus magis proportionales, & figuram ad formam Ellipseos umbilicum in concursu radiorum habentis magis accedentem, si corpus maximum his attractionibus agitetur, quam si maximum illud vel a minoribus non attractum quiescat, vel multo minus vel multo magis attractum aut multo minus aut multo magis agitetur. (In a three-body system under inverse-square-like attractions with certain reciprocity conditions, the inner body's orbit and area-time proportionality approach elliptic form more closely when the massive body is acted upon by the smaller ones in a certain balanced way than when it is fixed or otherwise differently perturbed.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed case analysis: Case 1 — two small bodies P & Q orbit a large S; define mediating distances and decompose attractions into components; show how additional accelerative attractions perturb the inner orbit from an exact ellipse and affect area proportionality, and that minimization of the disturbing attractions MN (i.e., balanced attractions toward Q) minimizes perturbation. Case 2 — small bodies orbit in different planes: additional components produce latitude perturbations. Corollaries: (1) inner body's motion minimally perturbed when the massive body's attractions on minors are balanced; (2) speed variations near conjunction/opposition vs quadratures: faster near conjunction/opposition; (3) geometric consequences on orbit curvature and maximum separation; (4) central body's centripetal force variation effect on period and apsidal motion; (5) apsidal advance/regress depends on these perturbations leading to long-term secular changes. (Q.E.D.)
